preview: Interview experience for Technology Analyst Intern at Morgan Stanley covering the online assessment, technical and HR rounds, key takeaways, and preparation tips.
content: MORGAN STANLEY TECHNOLOGY ANALYST INTERN INTERVIEW EXPERIENCE YEAR - 2024 SARID QURESHI COMPUTER ENGINEERING BATCH - 2026 Overview Just two weeks before our Mid-Sem Tests, the Training and Placement Office (TPO) forwarded a message about an on-campus drive by Morgan Stanley. It was a complete surprise, as we hadn’t expected Morgan Stanley to come. The online assessment was scheduled for the 10th of September, and the interviews were on the 13th of September. The entire process from the internship drive announcement to the interview process and declaring the results took around 1 week. Eligibility Criteria 1. Circuital Branch Student 2. CGPA ≥7.5 3. No Backlogs Online Assessment (OA) Platform - SHL AMCAT (No Proctoring) Duration - 2 Hours The Online Assessment was conducted on 10th September on the SHL AMCAT Platform. The duration was around 2 hours and there were three sections and each section was separately timed. You cannot skip a section unless you complete it fully or the timer runs out. The three sections appeared in the following order: ● Aptitude Section - 36 mins ● Debugging Section - 20 mins ● Coding Section - 60 mins Aptitude Section - 24 Questions ● This section was the most difficult and deciding factor for clearing the OA, considering the time allowed per question and the calculations involved in most of them. ● Individual questions did not have a time limit, the whole section was to be completed in 36 mins. ● Attempting each question was compulsory and previously attempted questions cannot be revisited. There was no negative marking. ● I attempted most of the questions and randomly selected the last few due to time constraints. The Topics ranged from: 1. Permutations and Combinations 2. Task ordering 3. Statistics 4. Pattern matching 5. Data interpretation 6. Logical reasoning Debugging Section - 7 Questions ● Before starting this section, you had an option to select your preferred language among C++ and Java (I preferred python but it was not available. In such cases, knowledge of diverse languages can come handy). ● This Section involved 7 easy debugging questions. ● I was able to answer 5 questions completely. Coding Section - 3 Questions 1. N encrypted integers were given, requiring us to decrypt them by multiplying all the numbers together to get their product, then Identifying the distinct prime factors of this product and finally returning the distinct prime factors as the decrypted message. 2. A string representing request IDs for resources was given which included characters from lowercase english alphabet. Out of the 26 types of resources, the highly demanded resources were denoted by the vowels (a, e, i, o, u). We had to find and return the longest sequence of requests for these highly demanded resources without repetition. 3. This problem focused on optimizing stage lighting for a play, using an N x M matrix to represent light intensity of the stage, where positive values indicated bright spots and negative values indicated dark spots. The light intensity for a particular section was calculated by the sum of all of the intensities in that section. We were also given the maximum light intensity, and the goal was to identify sections of the stage that satisfied this limit. Results: This concluded the Online Assessment and the result was declared on 12th September around 6:00 PM (The day before the interview). 23 students were shortlisted for interviews. Interview Day Date: 13 September 2024 Venue: Virtual (Zoom) Round 1: Technical Interview (Duration: 1 hr) I was the first to be interviewed at 8:00 AM. There were two very experienced interviewers for the first round. One was the VP and the other was a Senior manager. They began by introducing themselves, then asked me to introduce myself (For this part, include the technical things about yourself that you would like the interviewer to know. Oftentimes they ask follow up questions depending on your introduction.) The VP started by asking my opinion on compiled v/s interpreted languages and which one I would prefer and the difference between them. She also provided her opinion on why she likes compiled languages more. Then she asked for conditions under which compiled language would be better than an interpreted language and vice versa. Then she asked about one of my projects in detail and what tech stack did I use and why? Why this project? What were my Learnings, and so on. Then she asked some questions based on OOPS which included classes, inheritance and constructors. Then the Senior manager followed by asking a DSA question which involved creating a custom Stack class with the functionality of get_min, get_second_min, and get_max and more. The focus was on testing the important aspects like code readability and functionality. Then the VP followed by asking about the internal working of built-in functions that I had used in my code (It is important to understand what is happening internally). She then followed by asking how the inbuilt sort() is implemented and what algorithm it uses under the hood in python. I explained the answer to her and then she asked about the working of Merge Sort in detail. The Senior Manager then followed by asking OS questions related to processes, multi-threading, and how it is used, deadlocks and so on. I drew the process state diagram on the whiteboard and explained to him the various states and transitions in detail. He seemed satisfied with the answer. The VP followed by asking questions related to DBMS. She gave an Employee schema and asked to query the employee with the second highest salary. Then she asked for alternate solutions to that query. This was followed by questions related to subqueries in DBMS. Then she asked questions related to altering the table once created, modifying the table, followed by creating constraints on attributes on table creation, followed by triggers in SQL. She asked to write SQL queries for all of the above questions. Then she followed by asking how autocomplete is implemented in our code editors. I tried several approaches and eventually got to using the Trie Data structure. Then, I once again got on the whiteboard and explained to her my approach using the Trie data structure and gave several examples. Both the interviewers seemed satisfied with the answers. Then they asked if I had any questions for them (always ask questions, it shows your interest in the company). I asked several questions and the round was over. Before ending the interview, the VP said “We don’t usually say this from our side, but the response is positive. We hardly found you wrong”. This felt like a moment of relief and I started preparing for the HR round. The interview lasted for one hour. Out of 23 candidates, 9 were selected to proceed to the next round. Round 2: Technical + HR (Duration: 45 mins) ● This round was scheduled at 2:00 PM and it aimed to assess my personality, strengths, weaknesses, capability to handle the role, background, and overall fit for the job. The interviewer was again a very experienced person who had been working for a long time within the organization. ● The interviewer began by introducing himself and the technologies that he had been working on in the organization and asked me to introduce myself. ● As I had mentioned in my introduction that I am an active hackathon participant, he asked several standard HR questions related to working with a team and the conflicts that arise in such cases like “do you like to work alone or in a team? and why?”, “What would you do if a team member is not working?”, “What would you do if two people in the team have differing opinions?”, and so on. ● He then moved to asking about the difference between a normal python list and a numpy array. Then he asked about the difference between a cpp array and a numpy array and the internal representation of both of them. This discussion went on for some time. ● Then he asked me to share my screen and guided me in writing a cpp code related to pointers. He dictated what to write and then started explaining the working of dynamic pointers in cpp related to typecasting. ● Then he asked whether I’m open to learning new technologies as it is not necessary that we would get to work on a tech stack that we are familiar with and it depends on the requirements of the organization. ● He followed up with personal questions such as: 1. What are your hobbies? 2. Where do you live? Are you a local resident or a hostelite? 3. How long does your commute take? ● Finally, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked several questions and the round was over. This round lasted for around 45 mins. Results were announced at 8 PM. Out of 9 candidates, 8 were selected, and I was fortunate to be among them. Key takeaways: 1. You must be able to answer a question on every single word that you’ve put on your resume. Create a resume with a high ATS score. Consult with your seniors or peers or use various online resources available. 2. During interviews, communicate your thought process clearly. Speaking out loud while solving problems not only helps interviewers follow your logic but also gives them the opportunity to provide hints if you're heading in the wrong direction. 3. Ask as many questions as needed and clarify the question so that you know you have understood the requirements correctly. Consider every edge case before proposing a solution. Don’t give the interviewer a chance to point out an edge case. 4. Make sure to cover other concepts like OOPS, OS, DBMS, basic HLD and LLD. 5. Give Mock interviews. Reach out to Seniors, or your peers, or use online resources available. 6. Read through other candidates’ interview experience. It will provide valuable insights, as interview formats are often similar across companies. This will help you better understand what to expect and how to approach different interview stages. Preparation Tips 1. Practice questions from Leetcode and GFG. You can also follow any sheet. The ones I mainly used were: Neetcode 150 and Striver’s sheet. 2. The questions asked in OA are mostly similar to Competitive Programming questions and are phrased deliberately to trick you. Although It is not necessary, having some experience in Competitive programming will give you an extra edge and you will not be afraid of any new questions you might get. 3. If the test contains Aptitude questions, they generally include Probability, PnC, Logic-based, Statistics, Math based puzzles, etc. Practice some questions from Geeksforgeeks or IndiaBix. 4. Commit to solving at least one or two problems daily to maintain a steady pace and avoid falling behind. Staying consistent is key. 5. Give contests on Leetcode, Codechef, Codeforces, whenever you can. 6. Go through past interview experiences, as they can offer valuable insights into the interview format and types of questions asked. 7. Discuss problems and approaches with friends or peers to learn new techniques and discover questions or methods you may not have considered. 8. Avoid comparing your progress with others. Focus on your personal growth and trust the preparation process that works best for you. Resources ● For DSA - Neetcode.io, GeeksForGeeks, Leetcode. ● For CP - Codeforces, Codechef. ● For OS - Gate Smashers playlist, InterviewBit-Questions. ● For DBMS - Gate Smashers Playlist, InterviewBit-Questions. ● For OOPS - GeeksForGeeks, OOPS by love babbar. ● For Puzzle - Coding Ninjas, GeeksForGeeks ● For System Design - Keerti Purswani Behind The Scenes Till now, you’ve read the entire process it takes to get selected in a company. Hectic, right? Now imagine doing that entire process not once, not twice, not five times, but seven times!! Yes, you read that right. It took me 7 companies and loads of interviews to land this internship at Morgan Stanley. Every rejection felt like a hurdle I had to jump over, but each one only made me more determined to reach the finish line. Reflecting on my journey, the path wasn’t easy — it was filled with challenges and setbacks. Before MS, I had given 12 interviews and reached the final rounds for some of the most prestigious companies: DE Shaw, Google, Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan Chase, Bank of New York, and Hilti. Each of these opportunities felt like a step closer to my dream, but the rejections that followed were heartbreaking. The feeling of being so close, yet falling short, is one that’s hard to describe. After every rejection, I would replay the interviews in my head, wondering what I could have done differently. The final round often feels like a cliffhanger — a point where everything you’ve worked for hangs in balance, only to be met with a “NO”. It was disheartening, but I knew I couldn’t let it define me. It took me not 3, not 5, not 8, not even 10, but 14 interviews across 7 companies to finally land at Morgan Stanley. Each rejection felt like a mountain to climb, but I kept going, knowing that every step brought me closer to my goal. Through these experiences, I learned a lot about myself and the process. Every rejection taught me something new: a technical skill I needed to improve, a behavioral question I should’ve answered differently, or even the importance of staying calm under pressure. These experiences were not failures — they were stepping stones that prepared me for what was to come. Luck plays a significant role in interviews, and it’s important to acknowledge that. There were moments where my preparation was perfect, yet the questions didn’t align with my strengths. Sometimes, it’s just about being at the right place at the right time or having the right interviewer who resonates with your answers. Accepting this aspect of luck helped me move forward without being overly critical of myself. To those reading this, I want to say: don’t let rejection discourage you. They are a part of the process, and every interview is a learning experience. Take notes, analyze what went wrong, and use it to come back stronger. Most importantly, believe in yourself. You are more than a single interview — you are the sum of your efforts, your learnings, and your persistence. Throughout this journey, one of the most significant factors that kept me motivated was surrounding myself with positive and supportive people. These individuals not only encouraged me during tough times but also pushed me to become the best version of myself. They reminded me of my potential when I doubted myself and celebrated my small victories along the way. It’s often said, "You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with". Being around driven and optimistic people helped me maintain focus, stay motivated, and continue striving for my goals. To anyone reading this, I urge you to reflect on your circle. Surround yourself with people who inspire you, who challenge you to grow, and who believe in your dreams. The right support system can make all the difference in turning setbacks into comebacks and dreams into reality. All this yapping is to conclude that If I can do it, so can you! Keep striving, keep learning, and remember: the right opportunity will find its way to you when the time is right. If you have any questions regarding my interview experience or need advice on interview preparation, feel free to reach out to me at saridqureshi299@gmail.com. I’ll be happy to help you. ALL THE BEST !!!
